N.45.summary: Ferdinand the Catholic to his ambassador Jerónimo de Vich in Rome: a long complaint against Julius II (the new cardinals, the absolution of the Venetians, the Pope's refusal of his counsel) and instructions to press the Emperor-Venice concord, settle Ferrara and deliver orders to Fabrizio Colonna. The decode is mechanical, unread groups in brackets.
N.45.en:
Because of what you, Jeronimo de Vich, wrote to me on [..] March, [?I understood] the [..] of the affairs there [..]
[..] for Mantua; and then straight afterwards came the publication of the nine cardinals whom the Pope created, and
this [..] much, of [..] not content with [..] that the Pope will not follow my counsel in the things that matter for
him and for the See of the Church, nor in the others [?has] any regard for me. For I have sent to beg him with much
[..] to take care to preserve and not to risk his favour, and to press the conclusion of the peace between the
Emperor [and] the Venetians; and [..] after [saying] that he would do so, he has done the contrary in [..] troops to
La Bastia, [..] few and [..] badly provided, from which has followed the rout you speak of, which [..] war [..] [..],
which has been no [..], which no [?harm], and [..] favour for all his business.

N.57.summary: The aftermath of Ravenna: Ferdinand reconstructs how Vich's letters and the papal side pushed the viceroy Ramón de Cardona into battle against his orders, tells Vich not to do it again, and asks that the Ferrara business be treated secretly, 'sin que la sienta el Papa'.
N.57.en:

continually wrote to them, pressing them on each one of them with very great [..] on behalf of [..] [their] captain
general, a very principal [man], [were] that they should not carry out what I had sent to tell them in so many
letters. And given how earnestly you wrote to me before the battle that on no account was it fitting that they should

N.60.summary: Written from the Navarre campaign: a reproach to Julius II for not paying his troops as the League requires, and the plan for the Sforza restoration in Milan, Massimiliano son of Duke Ludovico to be put into the state by the Emperor's hand.
